Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open. For coefficients $a_{ij},b_i,c_i,d$ on $U$, define the positive divergence-form operator
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^d D_i(a_{ij}D_j u)+\sum_{i=1}^dD_i(b_i u)+\sum_{i=1}^d c_iD_i u+du.$$
When the coefficients are continuously differentiable where needed, its nondivergence expansion is
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^d a_{ij}D_iD_j u+\sum_{j=1}^d\widetilde b_jD_j u+\widetilde c\,u,$$
with
$$\widetilde b_j=\sum_{i=1}^dD_i a_{ij}+b_j+c_j,\qquad \widetilde c=\sum_{i=1}^dD_i b_i+d.$$
The **positive divergence convention** here means that the principal part is $+\sum_{i,j}D_i(a_{ij}D_j u)$. This sign is part of the definition.

derivations.claim:
Since $U$ is bounded, choose real numbers $a_1<b_1$ with $a_1\le x_1\le b_1$ on $\bar U$. Let $B=\|\widetilde b_1\|_{C^0(U)}$ and $C_0=\|\widetilde c\|_{C^0(U)}$. Choose $\kappa>0$ large enough that $\kappa^2\lambda_0-\kappa B-C_0\ge1$. For $\psi(x)=e^{\kappa x_1}$, [F1] gives
$$L[\psi](x)=e^{\kappa x_1}\bigl(\kappa^2a_{11}(x)+\kappa\widetilde b_1(x)+\widetilde c(x)\bigr)\ge e^{\kappa a_1}>0.$$
Choose $M>e^{\kappa b_1}$ and set $\Phi=M-\psi$. Then $\Phi>0$ on $\bar U$ and $L[\Phi]=M\widetilde c-L[\psi]\le-e^{\kappa a_1}$.

Put $R=\|L[w]\|_{C^0(U)}$, $Q=\|w\|_{C^0(\partial U)}$, and $\eta=e^{\kappa a_1}$. For $z=w-Q-(R/\eta)\Phi$, the boundary values satisfy $z\le0$. In $U$,
$$L[z]=L[w]-Q\widetilde c-(R/\eta)L[\Phi]\ge -R+R=0,$$
because $-Q\widetilde c\ge0$.

Suppose $z(x_0)>0$ at some $x_0\in U$. Since $z\le0$ on $\partial U$ and $z$ is continuous on $\bar U$, its positive maximum is attained at an interior point. For sufficiently small $\delta>0$, $z+\delta\psi$ has an interior positive maximum as well: its value at $x_0$ is at least $z(x_0)>0$, while its boundary values are at most $\delta e^{\kappa b_1}<z(x_0)$. At that interior maximum [F2] and $\widetilde c\le0$ give $L[z+\delta\psi]\le0$, contradicting $L[z+\delta\psi]>0$. Hence $z\le0$ on $U$, and therefore
$$w\le Q+(R/\eta)\|\Phi\|_{C^0(\bar U)}.$$
Applying the same argument to $-w$ yields the corresponding lower bound. Taking $C_L=\max\{1,\|\Phi\|_{C^0(\bar U)}/\eta\}$ proves the first estimate; applying it to $u^*-h$ proves the second.

$$[v]_{\alpha;E}=\sup_{x\ne y\in E}\frac{|v(x)-v(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
